description:
We are a dedicated team of engineering students planning to build something related to the medical field in space. Our strengths are in engineering, biology, problem- solving, product planning, design, and presentation. 

What we are missing is a strong programmer experience with Python, JavaScript, or React, along with some familiarity with APIs or backend work, but we value curiosity and reliability just as much as technical skill.
summary: We built a screening aid for autonomous astronaut health monitoring on long missions. It follows ten indicators, including bone markers (CTX, P1NP, sclerostin), blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, glucose and sleep. Instead of one fixed limit, we compare each reading with the astronaut’s own expected spaceflight adaptation curve and uncertainty band. The tool stays quiet during expected early changes, needs a pattern to persist before alerting, and combines indicators, for example bone formation and resorption moving apart. A body diagram shows normal, watch, yellow and red status, and every alert has a plain-language “why”. It addresses the Distance from Earth and Altered Gravity hazards by supporting self-assessment when real-time medical help is limited. NASA currently has no in-flight bone measurement, so early markers matter. Real astronaut data is not public, so every reading is simulated and labelled. In 200 simulated astronauts, it raised about 1.8 alerts per astronaut per 180-day mission, against about 9 for a fixed 3-of-5 rule. 53 of 146 parameter groups are still unsourced placeholders, shown live in the app. It runs fully offline in the browser, with no backend. It is decision support, not a diagnostic device, and we would validate it first in Earth-based bed-rest studies.
details:
What it does and how it works:
We built an astronaut health self-assessment dashboard. Each astronaut gets a personal baseline from pre-flight values. Real astronaut baselines aren’t accessible to us, so we simulate them from distributions based on published pre-flight data. We compare each reading with the astronaut’s expected spaceflight adaptation curve and its uncertainty band, which the app learns from that astronaut’s own readings. A quiet period early in flight shows only “watching”. An alert needs 3 of the last 5 readings outside the band (2 of 3 for bone markers), and related indicators can raise a level only when one of them is already flagged, for example bone formation and resorption moving apart. Fixed safety lines fire immediately, with a repeat-reading check for blood pressure, heart rate and glucose. The output is a status on a body diagram (normal, watch, yellow, red), a trend chart and a plain-language explanation of why. Yellow suggests checking and repeating; red suggests notifying the flight surgeon. We track bone markers (CTX, P1NP, sclerostin), blood pressure, heart rate, resting and exercise temperature, glucose and sleep. The chart also shows each marker’s Reference Change Value, which accounts for normal biological variation.

Benefits:

  • Supports astronaut autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed or support is limited.
  • Looks for persistent drift during the mission, which pre- and post-flight checks cannot do. NASA currently has no in-flight bone density measurement.
  • Uses personal baselines, so each astronaut is their own control.
  • Explains readings in simple language, without needing medical expertise.

Intended impact:
To help crews and flight surgeons notice physiological changes early and act on them (exercise, nutrition, medical review) on future long-duration and deep-space missions.

Tools and technology:

  • The published papers are cited on the Sources page. We built on published spaceflight literature, much of it from NASA. The expected curves, spreads and limits come from NASA Human Research Program evidence reports (bone fracture 2024, cardiovascular 2022, muscle and aerobic capacity 2024, sleep), the NASA crew health standard NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, NASA SP-2009-3405, and peer-reviewed studies by NASA scientists on ISS astronauts (for example Smith et al. 2005-2015, Sibonga et al. 2019, Platts et al. 2009), together with other spaceflight studies listed on the Sources page. We entered their summary numbers by hand; a few were read by eye from published figures, and each value’s caveat says how it was obtained. No raw per-astronaut NASA data files are bundled. Values with no published source are marked as placeholders (53 of 146 parameter groups at submission), and the app’s header shows how many remain. The app is built with React, TypeScript and Vite, with a pure-TypeScript engine, tested with Vitest. It runs fully offline in the browser with no backend and is deployed on Vercel. We tested it on 200 simulated astronauts: about 1.8 alerts per astronaut per 180-day mission, against about 9 for a fixed 3-of-5 rule.

NASA sources used:

  • Barger LK, et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:904–912
  • Platts SH, et al. Aviat Space Environ Med 2009;80(5 Suppl):A29-A36, Table I
  • McPhee JC, Charles JB (eds). Human Health and Performance Risks of Space Exploration Missions. NASA SP-2009-3405, 2009.
  • Sibonga JD, King L. Evidence Report: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone. NASA HRP-F07-ERFT.R2, 2024 (NTRS 20240005190).
  • Smith SM, et al. J Bone Miner Res 2014;29(7):1639-1645, Tables 2-3.
  • Smith SM, et al. J Bone Miner Res 2012;27(9):1896-1906, Table 4.
  • Smith SM, et al. J Bone Miner Res 2005;20(2):208-218, Table 5.
  • NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 Revision C, 2023.
  • Smith SM, et al. Bone 2015;81:712-720, Tables 1-2.
  • Sibonga J, et al. Bone 2019;128:112037, Table 4.
  • NASA HRP Evidence Report: Risk of Impaired Performance Due to Reduced Muscle Mass, Strength & Endurance and Reduced Aerobic Capacity, 2024.
  • NASA HRP Evidence Report: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes, 2022.
  • NASA HRP Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload.

Rather than relying on one biomarker, the design combines indicators and compares each against the astronaut’s own baseline. It does not depend on one device: readings enter through a single adapter layer (simulated, manual entry or file import). It is also transparent: every simulated value is labelled, and every parameter is tied to a published source or flagged as a placeholder, a design choice or a simulator assumption.

Factors we considered:

  • Evidence quality. Sclerostin is a plausible marker but has limited direct in-flight data, so it is used as part of a panel, flagged for monitoring only and never above yellow.
  • Sample type. Urinary and serum values aren’t mixed.
  • Resting and exercise temperature are treated separately.
  • Fluid redistribution, jugular flow and SANS are out of scope for this version and listed as future work.
  • Data availability: real astronaut data is limited, so simulation is clearly labelled.
  • It is a decision-support concept, not a diagnostic device, and would be validated first in Earth-based bed-rest studies.
